strings.fig.label: FIG.
strings.fig.01.title: Dependency ratio: old age pension beneficiaries per employed person
strings.fig.01.caption: Contributory pensioners divided by contributing affiliates, month by month since 1996.
strings.fig.01.limit: A high ratio does not say who pays: it counts heads, not euros.
strings.fig.01.definition: Counts beneficiaries of old age pensions (Eurostat, persons) divided by employed persons aged 15 to 64 (Eurostat, labour force survey). Excludes survivor and disability pension beneficiaries from the numerator and non-employed persons from the denominator.
strings.fig.02.title: Public pension expenditure (% of GDP)
strings.fig.02.caption: Public pension expenditure as a share of GDP, year by year.
strings.fig.02.limit: A share of GDP measures effort: it does not say whether contributions cover the bill.
strings.fig.02.definition: Counts total public pension expenditure as a share of gross domestic product, all pension functions and all schemes, Spain. Excludes social expenditure that is not a pension.
strings.fig.03.title: Cohort return
strings.fig.03.caption: Internal rate of return for a representative cohort: paid in against drawn out, with its band.
strings.fig.03.limit: The return depends on life expectancy and payment count: both are shown beside it.
strings.fig.03.definition: Counts the internal rate of return of a representative cohort: contributions paid over the contributing years against pensions drawn over the expected years of retirement. Excludes survivor and disability benefits and taxes.
strings.fig.04.title: Implicit debt at four rates
strings.fig.04.caption: Present value of accrued obligations minus system assets, at four discount rates.
strings.fig.04.limit: The discount rate is a choice: that is why all four are published.
strings.fig.04.definition: Counts the present value of accrued pension obligations minus the Fondo de Reserva balance, at four discount rates. Excludes future accrual and assets other than the Fondo de Reserva.
strings.fig.05.title: Required base growth
strings.fig.05.caption: Growth of the contributor base needed to pay the promised return, against the projected growth.
strings.fig.05.limit: It is not a forecast: it is the difference between two stated assumptions.
strings.fig.05.definition: Counts the contributor-base growth the scheme must sustain to pay the cohort return it promises, minus the projected growth of that base. Excludes migration effects and employment-policy effects.
strings.fig.06.title: Contributory dependency ratio
strings.fig.06.caption: Contributory pensions in force divided by contributing affiliates, month by month.
strings.fig.06.limit: It counts every contributory pension, not only the old age ones.
strings.fig.06.definition: Counts all contributory pensioners in force in Spain (jubilación, viudedad, incapacidad, orfandad) divided by contributing affiliates in employment. Excludes non-contributory pensions and persons who do not contribute.
strings.fig.07.title: Contribution cover
strings.fig.07.caption: Social contributions divided by contributory pension expenditure, year by year.
strings.fig.07.limit: Cover below 1 does not measure the debt: it measures that year’s shortfall.
strings.fig.07.definition: Counts social contributions divided by contributory pension expenditure. Excludes transfers from general taxation and debt.
strings.fig.03.reason: No internationally comparable source for average contributions.
strings.fig.04.reason: No internationally comparable source for accrued obligations and system assets.
strings.fig.05.reason: Depends on the cohort return, which has no internationally comparable computation.
strings.fig.06.reason: The national figure needs contributory pensioners and contributing affiliates. They are not available in this deployment.
strings.fig.07.reason: The national figure needs social contributions and contributory pension expenditure. They are not available in this deployment.

strings.assumptions.entryAge.label: Entry age
strings.assumptions.entryAge.consequence: Fixes the contributing years that enter the return.
strings.assumptions.retirementAge.label: Retirement age
strings.assumptions.retirementAge.consequence: Closes working life and opens the payout.
strings.assumptions.pagas.label: Annual payments
strings.assumptions.pagas.consequence: Fourteen payments raise the annual pension over twelve.
strings.assumptions.lifeExpectancy.label: Life expectancy at 65
strings.assumptions.lifeExpectancy.consequence: Each extra year lowers the cohort return.
strings.assumptions.inflation.label: Annual inflation
strings.assumptions.inflation.consequence: Turns the nominal return into a real return.
strings.assumptions.gWage.label: Real wage growth
strings.assumptions.gWage.consequence: Subtracted from the return to obtain required growth.
strings.assumptions.discountRates.label: Discount rates
strings.assumptions.discountRates.consequence: One, two, three and four per cent: the set is always complete.
strings.assumptions.horizon.label: Projection horizon

strings.assumptions.freshness.consequence: Outside it the computation fails instead of reusing the snapshot.

agreement.text: Pension expenditure has grown in nominal terms over the last decade according to Eurostat's harmonised series.
The population aged 16 to 64 that INE projects shrinks between 2026 and 2070.

positions.name: Funded by contributions
positions.quote: Contributory pensions are paid out of the system's social contributions.

positions.name: Requires transfers
positions.quote: Part of pension expenditure is covered by transfers from the State.

thesis.statement: If the promised return exceeds the growth of the base, the difference can only be paid with more contributions, lower pensions or debt.
paragraphs: Read coldly, the scheme resembles a pyramid: what comes in today pays what was promised yesterday, and the promise holds only while the base grows.
This is neither an accusation nor a forecast. It is the arithmetic consequence of comparing two numbers this page computes and publishes.
